meta.source: Beverage Culture Analysis: Category Signals in the U.S. Beverage Industry (expanded U.S. edition)
meta.note: Category backdrop for the analysis closing. Direction and shape only, no figures and no brand names, so the firewall holds. Refresh when a new report is published. Keys match the brand subCategory tags in taxonomy.js.

vodka.posture: Mature and slowly shrinking, but still a workhorse for mixing. It is losing casual occasions to canned cocktails, smaller formats, and non-alcoholic options, and the softness runs across every price tier.

gin.posture: A small, contracting category overall, while the higher-end, cocktail-driven end still holds an audience. It performs when there is a clear reason to choose it, not from sitting on the shelf.

rum.posture: A weak middle with a small premium bright spot. Everyday mixing rum is fading while a narrow group of drinkers trades up to more serious, higher-priced bottles.

tequila.posture: Cooling after years of fast growth rather than reversing. Drinkers are still in agave spirits, but spending is shifting down toward more accessible bottles after a long premium run.

mezcal.posture: Reported together with tequila. Agave spirits are normalizing after fast growth, with spending moving toward more accessible tiers rather than the category unwinding.

whiskey.posture: A large heritage family settling into a mature phase. Heritage and scarcity stories no longer guarantee trade-up, and the market is more cautious and more disciplined about inventory.

scotch.posture: Prestige is intact but pressured. Committed single-malt drinkers still value provenance, while imported Scotch is exposed to tariffs, exchange rates, and slower restocking.

bourbon.posture: One of the more resilient corners of whiskey, holding demand better than its peers. The new challenge is abundance: a large aging supply now has to be sold through rather than chased.

wine.posture: In a multi-year correction, not a one-year dip. It has lost some of its automatic default status, and strong and weak producers are pulling apart, with direct hospitality relationships carrying the healthy ones.

beer.posture: Structurally smaller, not just having an off year. It is no longer the automatic choice for every casual occasion, though hospitality-driven and local models hold up better, and non-alcoholic beer is a real bright spot.

rtd.posture: A permanent, growing part of the market that churns fast inside. Spirits-based and wine-based cans are rising while hard seltzer fades, and single-serve, same-day buying drives it.

non-alc.posture: Fast-growing and now mainstream, working as an addition to drinking rather than a replacement. Most buyers also buy alcohol and switch by occasion.

thc.posture: Demand is rising fast while the legal ground stays unstable. Treat the momentum as real interest, with regulation as the wild card that can change the picture quickly.

liqueur.posture: Broadly soft as a group, but it is cocktail architecture as much as a standalone pour, so flavor families move differently. Value comes when a product clearly serves a specific drink or occasion.

amaro.posture: A small, culturally influential niche with no clean public sales read, so it is judged by menu placements, reorders, and staff-led trial rather than category size. It punches above its shelf footprint in cocktail-forward programs.

brandy.posture: A pressured family, including Cognac and Armagnac, with declines reaching even the higher tiers. It stays relevant in cocktails, gifting, and after-dinner occasions, and is exposed to imported-prestige trade pressure.

coffee-tea.posture: Daily rituals that endure while formats fragment. Tea is soft by volume and coffee is more resilient, with cold brew and ready-to-drink formats growing as additions rather than replacing the morning cup.

energy.posture: A functional mainstream category that keeps growing and recruiting new occasions, expanding from performance into everyday focus, with zero-sugar and flavor-driven options leading.
